title: Hierarchical Bayesian Regression for Battery Capacity: Predicting New Cells and Retiring Them
text:
Series: Bayesian Modelling for Industrial Applications, Part 3, second post. The first post of Part 3 built a hierarchical Beta regression of battery state of health, with cells in chemistries, and checked its priors and how well it fits the cells of the data.
A manufacturer that introduces a new chemistry has tested only a few cells of it, and the operator of a battery fleet must decide at every inspection whether to retire a cell or leave it in service. The fit to cells that the model has seen says little about either. What matters is how well the model predicts a cell that it has never seen, and what that prediction is worth in the decision that it serves.
This post answers both on two cells that the model did not see, one of each chemistry. It states the decision of the operator first, then tests the hierarchy against one curve for all cells, one curve for each cell and a control that has no diagnostics, and finally turns each strategy into a retirement rule and compares what the rules cost. As a predictor of a new cell the hierarchy helps in one setting only, after the cell has shown its first 100 cycles, and as a retirement rule its value depends on the cost ratio of the operator.
Show the setup of the notebook
from importlib.metadata import version
import os
from pathlib import Path
import tempfile
import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "2")

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

from bayes import decision
from bayes.data import calce
from bayes.plot import change, concepts, hierarchy
from bayes.plot.inline import show
from bayes.regression import evaluate, hierarchical as hier

FAST = os.environ.get("HIER_FAST") == "1"  # a smoke test with a few draws, to check that the notebook runs
CACHE = Path("cache-fast" if FAST else "cache")
CACHE.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
FEATURES = ["charge_current_auc", "charge_current_mean", "discharge_voltage_auc", "discharge_voltage_crest"]
HELD_OUT = ["CS2_38", "CX2_38"]  # the last cell of each chemistry, kept back for the tests of new cells
SEEN = (0, 100, 300)  # cycles of a new cell that the model has seen
GAP = 50  # embargo, in cycles, between the cycles seen and the cycles scored
MAIN = {"draws": 40 if FAST else 500, "tune": 40 if FAST else 750, "chains": 2 if FAST else 4}
REFIT = {"draws": 40 if FAST else 500, "tune": 40 if FAST else 750, "chains": 2 if FAST else 4}
THRESHOLD = evaluate.END_OF_LIFE  # a cell below this state of health, in percent, is at its end of life
RATIOS = np.round(np.arange(0.02, 0.96, 0.02), 2)  # cost-loss ratios of the decision
PHI_PRIORS = {  # log-normal priors of the precision: the mean and standard deviation of its logarithm
    "Narrow": (float(np.log(100.0)), 0.3),  # centred on 100
    "Default": (float(np.log(100.0)), 1.0),  # centred on 100
    "Wide": (float(np.log(1000.0)), 1.5),  # centred on 1,000
}
print("pymc", version("pymc"), "| arviz", version("arviz"), "| fast mode:", FAST)

data = calce.load(Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "calce-battery-features.parquet", FEATURES, every=8)
train, held_out = calce.split(data, HELD_OUT)

for chemistry, rows in summary.groupby("CellType"):

        f"{chemistry}: {len(rows)} cells, {rows['rows'].min()} to {rows['rows'].max()} kept cycles per cell, longest life {rows['last_cycle'].max()} cycles"
    )

    f"{len(data):,} cycles kept; {len(train):,} in the {train['cell'].nunique()} training cells; held out: {', '.join(HELD_OUT)}"
)
print(f"SoH above 100%: {(data['soh'] > 100).mean():.1%} of the kept cycles")

title: Who Owns the Method in a Data Science Team
text:
Most people who have worked in an organisation have received an instruction that stated what the result should be and also how to obtain it. A leader who stood further from the work than the person who carried it out had written it. Such an instruction is usually well meant, since it saves a discussion and reflects a route that has worked before. Its effect on a capable team is nonetheless predictable. The team delivers what was specified and stops reporting what it sees, including the point at which the specified route fails. In a data science team the effect is stronger, because the route is the part of the work that is least known in advance. A brief that reads “build a random forest on these five features to predict churn by Friday” fixes the model, the inputs and the date before anyone has looked at the data.
In my experience of leading and working beside data science teams, this habit is a more persistent cause of disengagement than a shortage of technical skill or a weak infrastructure. The reason for the work, the outcome that it should achieve and the method that produces it are all settled at once, before the team has contributed. A team that may only carry out the prescription of someone else cannot do what it was hired to do, which is to find out what the data is able to say. Its members gradually cease to act as problem-solvers.
This post argues that the method should belong to the team, and that leadership should hold the reason and the outcome together with the constraints of the business. It sets out what a prescribed method costs. The second post turns the argument into a division of the work, states when a leader should specify the method after all, and describes three changes in practice. The argument rests on experience, on a small number of books on leadership and on three studies. It is not a measured result, and its limits are stated in the last section. The post also continues three earlier ones, on shared mental models, on group forces in organisational change and on the strategic kernel of an AI strategy. They supply the neighbouring arguments that are referred to below.

title: Choosing the Lookback Window, Lags and Inputs of a Forecaster
text:
Inputs of a Forecaster
Before a model predicts tomorrow’s load, someone has to decide what it may look at: how many recent observations to give it as a window, which older values to add beside them, and which other inputs, such as the hour, the weekday or the temperature, to include. These choices usually come from habit, a week of history because a week feels natural, or from trial and error on the test set, which lets the test period shape a model that is meant to be judged on it.
This post makes all three choices from the training data alone, using functions of the open-source library twiga.[1] The autocorrelation sets the window and proposes the lags. The lags, the calendar variables and the weather inputs are then ranked by six measures of relevance, first within each group and then together. A column of random noise sits among the candidates as a control, because a ranking that places noise high cannot be trusted. Four series with different character serve as examples: the half-hourly demand of one London household, the hourly charging of electric vehicles (EV) across Los Angeles, the output of a photovoltaic (PV) array, and the net load of the site that the array feeds.
No forecaster is trained, so the post makes no claim about accuracy. Its claim is narrower: the choices can be made without touching the test period, every step can be inspected, and the result behaves sensibly on a control. The code is folded under each figure, and every selection function is imported from twiga 1.1.8 and not rewritten.

GREY, GREY_DARK, FONT = "#CED4DA", "#6B7280", "'Libre Franklin', 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif"


def tint(colour: str, amount: float = 0.85) -> str:
    """A colour mixed with white, for bands and fills."""
    rgb = np.array([int(colour[i : i + 2], 16) for i in (1, 3, 5)])
    return "#" + "".join(f"{int(v):02X}" for v in rgb + (255 - rgb) * amount)


def house() -> theme:
    """Thin dark axes on the left and bottom, no grid, no legend, Libre Franklin type."""
    return theme(
        legend_position="none", plot_background=element_rect(fill="white", color="white"), panel_background=element_blank(),
        panel_border=element_blank(), panel_grid=element_blank(), strip_background=element_blank(),
        strip_text=element_text(face="bold", size=14, hjust=0), axis_line=element_line(size=0.5, color=INK),
        axis_ticks=element_line(size=0.5, color=INK), axis_ticks_length=4,
        text=element_text(family=FONT, size=13, color=INK), plot_margin=[8, 18, 4, 4],
    )


PHONE_WIDTH = 420
LAYOUT = {"phone": False}


def columns(desktop: int, phone: int = 1) -> int:
    """Panels in a row: ``desktop`` on a wide screen, ``phone`` in the narrow variant of a figure."""
    return phone if LAYOUT["phone"] else desktop


def size(width: int, height: int, panels: int = 1, ncol: int = 1, phone_ncol: int = 1) -> ggsize:
    """Canvas of a figure: as given on a wide screen, narrow with the panels re-stacked in the phone variant."""
    if not LAYOUT["phone"]:
        return ggsize(width, height)
    per_panel = (height - 60) / -(-panels // ncol)
    ratio = (PHONE_WIDTH / phone_ncol) / (width / ncol)
    return ggsize(PHONE_WIDTH, int(60 + -(-panels // phone_ncol) * per_panel * ratio * 1.15))


def inline(plot, kind: str) -> str:
    """The SVG of a figure as a block that scales with the page; ``kind`` marks the wide or the narrow variant."""
    svg = plot.to_svg()
    width, height = (float(v) for v in re.search(r'width="([\d.]+)" height="([\d.]+)"', svg).groups())
    svg = svg.replace(f'width="{width}" height="{height}"', f'viewBox="0 0 {width:g} {height:g}" width="100%"', 1)
    return f'<div class="letsplot letsplot-{kind}">{svg}</div>'


def show(build) -> None:
    """Draw a figure twice, wide and narrow, so that the page shows the variant that fits the width of the screen."""
    LAYOUT["phone"] = False
    wide = inline(build(), "desktop")
    LAYOUT["phone"] = True
    try:
        narrow = inline(build(), "phone")
    finally:
        LAYOUT["phone"] = False
    display(HTML(wide + narrow))


def note(frame: pd.DataFrame, colour: str = INK, hjust: float = 0.0, size: float = 5.6):
    """Direct labels from a frame with columns x, y, label (and the facet column), with a white halo over the marks."""
    return geom_text(
        aes("x", "y", label="label"), data=frame, color=colour, hjust=hjust, size=size, family=FONT,
        halo_width=2, halo_color="white", inherit_aes=False,
    )

Lookback Window and Lags
A forecaster that predicts the next day from what is known at the forecast origin draws on the history of its target in two ways. The lookback window is a block of the WW most recent observations, ending at the origin. A lag of kk steps adds the value yt−ky_{t-k}, which reaches further back than the window without making it longer. A lag can be used only if its value exists at the origin, so every lag is at least one step. Figure 2 shows a window, the horizon and three lags for a forecast one day ahead.
Each choice has a price. A window that is too short hides the daily shape, while a window that is too long, or a lag that repeats what the window already holds, hands the model the same information twice and raises its variance without adding signal. The autocorrelation function (ACF) gives a principled starting point.[5] It is the correlation of the series with itself kk steps earlier,
ρk=Cov⁡(yt,yt−k)Var⁡(yt),
\rho_k = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(y_t,\, y_{t-k})}{\operatorname{Var}(y_t)},

and its peaks fall at the periods in which the series repeats. The shortest significant peak sets the window, because it is the shortest span over which the dynamics repeat, and the longer peaks become lag candidates. A lag as long as the shortest period would only repeat the window, so it is left out. A value of ρk\rho_k counts as significant when it lies outside the band ±1.96/T\pm 1.96/\sqrt{T}, the range expected for a series of length TT with no autocorrelation.

All four series give the same answer, shown in Figure 3: a window of one day, the blue band, and lag candidates of two, three and seven days, the dots. The daily cycle that every series has produces it. Charging repeats most closely, with an autocorrelation of 0.88 at one day and −0.55-0.55 at half a day, where the load sits on the opposite side of the cycle. The PV array and the net load follow at 0.77 and 0.79. A single household repeats its day only loosely, at 0.35, and its autocorrelation at seven days, 0.42, is higher than at one day, which makes the week its stronger rhythm. All four stay well above the band of no autocorrelation, which is ±0.011\pm 0.011 to ±0.035\pm 0.035.
This step has a limit that is worth stating plainly. The candidates are calendar multiples of the detected period, so any series with a daily cycle receives the same list. The analysis points to where to look and does not search for a lag particular to one series. Choosing among the candidates, and between them and the other inputs, is the job of the ranking that follows.


Six Measures of Relevance
An input is relevant to the extent that it tells something about the target, and no single measure sees every kind of dependence. twiga therefore scores each candidate in six ways:

the absolute Spearman rank correlation, which detects any monotone relation;
the F statistic of a linear fit, which detects a linear relation;
the mutual information, which detects any relation visible in the joint histogram of the two variables;
Chatterjee’s ξ\xi, a rank-based coefficient that is zero under independence and one when one variable is a function of the other, whatever its shape;[6]
the predictive power score, the gain of a small decision tree fitted on the candidate alone over predicting the mean of the target;
the impurity importance of a random forest, which also picks up interactions between inputs.[7]

Consider a load that rises when the temperature departs from a comfortable value in either direction. The rank correlation and the F statistic cannot see that relation and the other four can, so a ranking built on one measure inherits the blind spot of that measure.
The six scores lie on different scales, so each is converted into a ranking and the rankings are combined, which is known as rank aggregation.[8] Under the Borda count a measure gives the best of mm candidates mm points, the next best m−1m-1 points, and so on, and the score of a candidate is its total over the measures. Writing rijr_{ij} for the points that measure jj gives candidate ii,
Bi=∑jrij.
B_i = \sum_{j} r_{ij}.

A sum like this counts measures that repeat each other twice. The rank correlation and the F statistic, for instance, usually order candidates alike. twiga therefore also offers a weighted sum, Si=∑jwjrijS_i = \sum_j w_j\, r_{ij}, in which the weight wjw_j is proportional to 1−ρ‾j1 - \bar{\rho}_j, where ρ‾j\bar{\rho}_j is the mean absolute Spearman correlation between the scores of measure jj and those of the other five. The weights have a floor of 0.05 and sum to one. The default of the library is the equal-weight sum, and the figures below use the weighted one, the option weighted_borda.
Two more choices complete the set-up. Each cyclic calendar variable enters as a sine and a cosine, so that 23:00 lies next to 00:00,[9] and a column of standard normal noise joins the candidates, since any measure that ranks it above a real input overstates relevance.

def xi_of(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Chatterjee's coefficient, floored at zero."""
    return max(float(_xicor_vector(a, b)[0]), 0.0)


def measure_scores(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray, group: np.ndarray | None) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Five relevance measures of one input on a scale from zero to one, and xi within each group when there are groups."""
    f = float(f_regression(a[:, None], b)[0][0])
    information = float(mutual_info_regression(a[:, None], b, random_state=0)[0])
    predictive = compute_ppscore(pd.DataFrame({"x": a, "y": b}), x="x", y="y", random_seed=0)["ppscore"]
    scores = {
        "Rank correlation": abs(float(spearmanr(a, b)[0])),
        "F statistic": f / (f + len(a) - 2),
        "Mutual information": float(np.sqrt(1.0 - np.exp(-2.0 * information))),
        "Chatterjee xi": xi_of(a, b),
        "Predictive power": float(predictive),
    }
    if group is not None:

def label(feature: str, name: str) -> str:
    """Sentence-case label of a candidate column."""
    days = lambda steps: f"{int(steps) // SERIES[name]['samples']} days"  # noqa: E731
    if "_lag_" in feature:
        return f"{NOUN[name]} {days(feature.rsplit('_', 1)[1])} earlier"
    if "_rolling_mean_win_" in feature:
        return f"Mean of the last {days(feature.rsplit('_', 1)[1])}"
    return FIELDS.get(feature, feature)


def design(name: str, share: float = TRAIN_SHARE) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, dict[str, list[str]], str]:
    """Candidate inputs of a series on its training window, in three subgroups, with a noise column as control."""
    series = SERIES[name]
    n, target = series["samples"], series["target"]
    _, days = lookback_and_lags(name, share)
    frame = AutoregressTransformer(
        n_samples=n, lags=days, windows=[days[0], days[-1]], window_funcs=["mean"], value_column=target
    ).fit_transform(training(name, share))
    frame = add_temporal_feature(frame, "timestamp")
    frame = add_fourier_features(frame, ["hour", "wday", "yday"], [24, 7, 366])
    frame["noise"] = np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal(len(frame))
    groups = {
        "Lags and means": [c for c in frame.columns if "_lag_" in c or "_rolling_" in c],
        "Calendar": [f"{field}_{kind}" for field in ("hour", "wday", "yday") for kind in ("sin", "cos")],
        "Known inputs": series["known"],
    }
    return frame.dropna(subset=[c for g in groups.values() for c in g] + ["noise", target]), groups, target


def rank(frame: pd.DataFrame, features: list[str], target: str, aggregation: str = "weighted_borda") -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, np.ndarray]:
    """twiga's six measures and their fusion for the given candidates; also the diversity weights of the measures."""
    _, scores = select_top_features(
        frame, features, target, top_k=len(features), alpha=None, include_chi2=False,
        rank_aggregation=aggregation, return_scores=True,
    )
    scores = scores.set_index("feature")
    return scores, diversity_weights(scores[RANKERS].fillna(0))


def pooled(name: str, share: float = TRAIN_SHARE) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, np.ndarray]:
    """One ranking of all the subgroups together and the noise column."""
    frame, groups, target = design(name, share)
    return rank(frame, [c for g in groups.values() for c in g] + ["noise"], target)

    """Compact row label for the subgroup panels: 2-day lag, 7-day mean, and the calendar and input labels."""

def group_panel(frame: pd.DataFrame, group: str, features: list[str], target: str, tag: str, height: int):
    """Rank within one subgroup, with the noise column as its control: a heat panel of the rank under each measure."""
    scores, _ = rank(frame, features + ["noise"], target, aggregation="borda_count")
    ranks = scores[RANKERS].fillna(0).rank(ascending=False, method="first").astype(int)
    order = scores["borda_count"].sort_values(ascending=False).index.tolist()
    m = len(order)

Figure 6: Ranking of the net load inputs within three subgroups, with the noise column as a control. Each tile is the position under one measure (Corr for the rank correlation, F, MI for the mutual information, Xi, PPS for the predictive power, RF for the forest importance), 1 is best and darkest, and the last column is the Borda total, where higher is better.




For the net load, the lag of two days heads the lags and means, ahead of the lags of seven and three days and the two means, with noise last. Among the calendar variables the sine of the hour is first, the cosine of the day of the year second and the cosine of the hour third. Both weekday encodings fall below the day of the year, and noise is last again. Among the known inputs the solar radiation comes first and the air temperature second, both ahead of the noise.
The three rankings could be used as they stand, with a fixed quota from each subgroup: the best two lags or means, the best two calendar variables and the best known input. Set against the single ranking of all candidates, which the next section builds, that rule selects the same inputs for the household and the EV charging, where it picks four, and shares three of five for the PV output and the net load. In those two series the quota keeps two calendar variables that rank seventh to ninth of fourteen once everything competes. It drops the lag of three days for the net load, which ranks third, and the panel temperature for the PV array, which ranks fourth. Every input it keeps still ranks above the noise column.

def per_group_rule(name: str) -> list[str]:
    """The best two lags or means, the best two calendar inputs and the best known input, each ranked within its subgroup."""
    frame, groups, target = design(name)
    picks = []
    for group, features in groups.items():
        if not features:
            continue
        scores, _ = rank(frame, features + ["noise"], target, aggregation="borda_count")
        ordered = [f for f in scores["borda_count"].sort_values(ascending=False).index if f != "noise"]
        picks += ordered[: 1 if group == "Known inputs" else 2]
    return picks


for name, (scores, _) in results.items():
    pooled_order = scores["weighted_borda"].sort_values(ascending=False).index.tolist()
    picks = per_group_rule(name)
    position = {f: pooled_order.index(f) + 1 for f in picks}
    below_noise = [label(f, name) for f in picks if position[f] > pooled_order.index("noise") + 1]
    print(f"{name}: per-subgroup picks {[label(f, name) for f in picks]}; positions in the pooled order {list(position.values())}; shared with the pooled top {len(picks)}: {len(set(picks) & set(pooled_order[: len(picks)]))}; below the noise column: {below_noise or 'none'}")




Pooled Ranking
Ranking everything together lets a lag compete with a calendar variable and a weather column on one scale. The ranking reads the first 70% of each series and uses the diversity-weighted sum. It covers twelve candidates for the household and the charging, and fourteen for the PV output and the net load.
Figure 7 draws the score of every candidate, best at the top, with the five best in blue and the noise column in orange. Five is only a convenient length. The dashed line marks the cut after the fifth, and the label gives the fall in score across it as a share of the range from best to worst.

The four orders differ in ways that follow the physics of each series.
In the household, the lag of seven days is first, the sine and cosine of the hour are second and third, and the lags of two and three days follow. The weekday encodings rank tenth and eleventh, so the household repeats by the week through its own past and not through a weekday variable. Noise is last of twelve under every measure except the forest importance, which puts it eighth.
For EV charging the order starts with the lags of seven and two days, then the sine of the hour, the cosine of the hour and the lag of three days. The two weekday encodings and the noise are the last three.
The irradiance leads the PV output under all six measures. The lags of two and three days come next, then the panel temperature and the lag of seven days. Noise ranks twelfth of fourteen, above both weekday encodings, which suits an array whose output does not depend on the day of the week.
In the net load the lags of two, seven and three days are followed by the solar radiation. The air temperature is only ninth, behind two means of the past and two calendar variables, and noise is last of fourteen.
Across the four series noise sits last or within the lowest three. The forest importance misplaces it most often, ranking it above real inputs in the household, the PV output and the net load, and the fusion corrects that, which is the practical case for combining measures. The cut at five is not equally firm everywhere. The score falls by 12.7% of the range after the fifth input for the EV charging, a real break, but by only 2.2%, 3.5% and 4.8% for the household, the PV output and the net load, where the sixth input is almost as relevant as the fifth. Inputs that score near the noise column, as the weekday encodings do, can be dropped without loss. Relevance alone does not remove redundancy, however: the sine and cosine of the hour sit side by side in two of the four shortlists, although a model needs the pair only to place the hour on a circle.

Figure 8 sets the default order of twiga, the equal-weight Borda count, against the diversity-weighted one. The two orders select the same five inputs in all four series, and their rank correlation lies between 0.99 and 1.00. On this evidence the weighting changes little, and equal weights are enough.

Limits of the Method
Relevance is not usefulness. Each measure scores one input at a time, so two inputs that carry the same information both rank high, and a shortlist can hold redundant inputs. The ranking is a shortlist for a forecaster to test and not a final choice. No forecaster is fitted here, so nothing shows that the shortlist forecasts better than all the candidates, and a comparison on held-out periods is the obvious next step, whose answer may differ by series. The weather inputs are treated as available over the forecast period, and with a real weather forecast their relevance would be lower.
The pool and the cut are fixed. The lags are calendar multiples of the detected period, so others, such as half-day multiples, are not in the pool, and the length of five is a convention. The selection reads the training window only, as the code here does. The function load_dataset of twiga applies the same functions to a whole file, which suits choosing a configuration for a dataset, whereas a backtest has to call them on the training window or the ranking sees the period that it is later tested on. Finally, the sample is small, since the findings describe one household, one site and one city and say nothing about how typical they are.


Recipe for Application
Every step uses the training window only.

Hold out the period to be forecast, and keep the first part of the series in time.
Find the periods of the series from its autocorrelation. The shortest sets the lookback window, and the longer ones become lag candidates, as get_best_autoregessive_features returns them.
List the candidates by kind: the lags and rolling means, the sine and cosine of each calendar cycle, and the inputs known in advance. Add a column of noise.
Rank each kind, then everything together. Keep the inputs that rank above the noise column and above a visible gap in the scores.
Pass the shortlist to a forecaster, and test it against the full set of candidates on held-out periods.



Summary of the Method
For all four series the autocorrelation gives a window of one day and lags of two, three and seven days, which the daily cycle explains. The ranking then separates them. The lag of seven days is the best input for the household and the EV charging, the lag of two days for the net load, and the irradiance for the PV output. The hour is the only calendar variable to reach a shortlist, and the weekday encodings are among the lowest everywhere. Noise ranks last or within the lowest three in every series, although the forest importance puts it above real inputs in three, more often than any other measure. The top five are the same under equal and diversity weights and across the first 50%, 70% and 90% of each series, though those windows are nested. Ranking each subgroup first and applying a fixed quota selects the same inputs as the combined ranking for the household and the EV charging, and weaker calendar inputs for the PV output and the net load.
The ranking is a shortlist to test, and its length is better read from the gaps between scores than fixed in advance. The notebook and the two small data files are in the repository of this site. The EV series is downloaded when the notebook runs, and the code needs twiga[ml]==1.1.8 and lets-plot.

title: The Missing Layer: How AI Business Models Capture Value
text:
In Parts 1 and 2, we saw that while 80% of organisations run AI pilots, only 5% actually get measurable value. Those posts argued that this gap is mostly about strategy; many AI projects fail because they lack a clear focus, a guiding policy, or targeted actions. That explanation is still true, but it is not the full picture.
Some organisations have followed the advice from Parts 1 and 2. They have a clear focus, a solid strategy, and well-planned pilots. Yet, they still struggle to turn these efforts into real business value. Having a strategy and roadmap is important, but it is not enough. What is missing is a strong business model.
Osterwalder and Pigneur [1] say a business model is how an organisation creates, delivers, and captures value. Strategy is about direction and navigation. The business model explains how value is created, who benefits, how it is delivered, and how the organisation keeps enough value to keep going. In most tech shifts, the difference between strategy and business model is clear. With AI, though, all three parts change at once, often in ways old business models cannot handle. Without a framework for this, even a good AI strategy might not lead to revenue, a lasting advantage, or a clear reason for the investment.
This post tackles that problem. The AI Business Model Innovation Framework helps turn strategy into a business model that really captures AI value. It does not replace the roadmap from Part 2, but works underneath it, filling in the gaps that a roadmap alone cannot cover.

title: The Strategic Kernel and the AI Strategy Gap
text:
AI investment is surging, driven by board mandates, competitive fear, and the pressure of not being left behind. Most organisations have very little to show for it. The pattern is familiar: a board asks for “an AI initiative,” a chatbot gets deployed, a launch gets celebrated, and the result gets called transformation.
The problem is not a lack of ambition. It is a confusion between wanting something and knowing how to get it. For example, “We will grow AI-driven revenue by 30%” is not a strategy. It is a goal. And when organisations commit technology budgets on the basis of a goal dressed up as strategy, they are not investing. They are hoping.
There is a framework that explains exactly why and what to do instead. Chapter 5 of Richard Rumelt’s Good Strategy / Bad Strategy [1] gets to the heart of this. Rumelt argues that a real strategy is a tool for overcoming obstacles, not a vision statement, not a goal, not a budget. He calls the structure behind it the strategic kernel. It has three elements that must work together: a diagnosis that names the real obstacle honestly, a guiding policy that decides how to attack it, and coherent actions that align every resource (money, people, time) in the same direction, as illustrated in Figure 1.
The kernel gives you the structure. But in The Crux [2], Rumelt adds a sharper demand: within your diagnosis, you must identify the crux, the one obstacle that, if removed, unlocks everything else. Most organisations sense where it lies. They just choose not to go there. Instead, they build strategy around it while the real obstacle sits untouched. In AI, the crux is rarely the model. It is the data quality the model cannot overcome, the decision rights no one wants to negotiate, or the workflow the technology has no way to integrate into.
Sometimes it is more fundamental still: the target itself is wrong. This happens in a recognisable pattern. Stakeholders frame problems as solutions: “we need a forecast model” rather than “we cannot meet demand”, and the actual obstacle never gets named. Technical teams, under pressure to deliver, do not push back on the problem statement. And organisations confuse using AI with solving problems with AI.
The result is a well-executed project aimed at the wrong thing: the model works, the metric it was built to move improves, and the business problem remains untouched.
Data quality, decision rights, workflow friction, wrong target: each is diagnosable before a line of code is written. Each is consistently avoided.
Nowhere is this more visible than in enterprise AI. Despite unprecedented investment, 80% of organisations are running pilots, yet only 5% have extracted measurable value [3], [4]. That gap is not a technology failure. It is a strategy failure. No honest diagnosis, no real guiding policy, just a list of initiatives dressed up as direction. Without the kernel, the crux goes unfound. The result is not merely effort pointed at the wrong problem. It is effort not pointed at anything at all.
What makes AI a particularly acute case is not a competence failure or an ambition failure. It is that AI has structural properties that actively resist each element of the kernel in ways that cloud adoption, ERP, or even the early internet did not. Understanding those properties, explored in the next section, is what separates a framework that produces a coherent AI strategy from one that merely looks like one.
The answer is technology roadmapping. A roadmap is not a project plan or a feature backlog. It is a structured framework that aligns market needs, business objectives, and technology capabilities across time [5]. As a strategic instrument, it forces the hard questions: why are we doing this, what are we building, and do we have what it takes [6]? When built around the kernel, it becomes the mechanism that translates diagnosis into direction and direction into coherent action.
This post, the first of two, explores how combining Rumelt’s strategic kernel with a structured technology roadmapping process [7], [8] can close that gap by giving organisations the tools to find the crux, build a guiding policy around it, and take actions that are genuinely coherent rather than merely busy. The second part puts the framework into practice with a five-step AI roadmapping process and a guide to spotting bad AI strategy before it costs you.

title: Individual Effort and Group Forces: Lewin’s Theory of Organisational Change
text:
Change is the only constant in today’s global business environment. Yet despite endless meetings, emails, and training sessions, many organizations still struggle to make change stick [1]. Leaders pour effort into motivating individuals, only to watch employees slip back into old habits.
The problem is not a lack of effort, it is a flaw in perspective. Too many change strategies focus on individuals, treating transformation as a personal mindset issue rather than a collective movement. It is the lone wolf approach to change: trying to inspire one person at a time while ignoring the social currents that shape behavior.
As social psychologist Kurt Lewin discovered decades ago, the real force behind sustainable change is not found in individual effort, it lies in the group dynamic, the pack. Understanding how groups form, interact, and influence one another can transform the way organizations lead change today.
This post revisits Lewin’s insights on group dynamics and explores how leaders can shift from managing people in isolation to mobilizing the collective energy of their teams.

At Analog Devices I design and run machine learning systems for supply chain planning and intelligent edge products, taking ideas from early prototypes to reliable production systems. Over the past decade I have worked across manufacturing, industrial, energy and semiconductor domains.
My technical work centres on probabilistic time series forecasting, Bayesian modelling and production MLOps. Alongside my industry role, I am active in research. title: Shared Mental Models: The Invisible Architecture of High-Performance Teams
text:
Ever been on a team where everything just clicks? communication is effortless, everyone knows their role, and the team anticipates each other’s moves, achieving goals with remarkable efficiency. This seamless collaboration is not a magic. It is often the result of something called a shared mental model, the invisible architecture that supports high-performance teamwork.
This post explores what shared mental models are, why they are a critical predictor of team effectiveness, and how leaders can consciously cultivate them, especially in the complex environments of virtual and hybrid teams.

title: From Framework to Practice: A Five-Step AI Roadmapping Process
text:
In Part 1, we explained why most AI strategies fail, highlighting that the issue goes beyond poor planning. AI presents three challenges: it reverses the typical diagnostic process, causes guiding policies to become outdated quickly, and creates value that standard measurement tools often overlook. As a result, many strategies lack an honest diagnosis and a real guiding policy, leaving only a list of initiatives that resemble a strategy but are not one.
We also demonstrated that integrating Rumelt’s strategic kernel with a structured technology roadmap creates a framework tailored to these challenges, rather than replicating outdated approaches. However, understanding the framework is only the beginning. The real challenge lies in applying it within an organisation’s constraints. This post addresses that challenge by presenting a five-step process for building an AI roadmap around the kernel and providing practical guidance for identifying when a strategy is lacking.
This post is intended for leaders already engaged with AI, such as CDOs, strategy leads, and senior executives who have invested in AI but have yet to see clear results. If your organisation is still considering AI investment, begin with Part 1. If you have invested and are struggling to achieve results, this post will help.

title: Hierarchical Bayesian Regression for Battery Capacity: Pooling across Cells and Chemistries
text:
Series: Bayesian Modelling for Industrial Applications, Part 3. Part 1 introduced Bayesian thinking, and Part 2 fitted one Beta regression to the six cells of one chemistry.
An operator of a battery fleet has to decide at every inspection whether to retire a cell or to leave it in service. A cell that has fallen below 80% of its nominal capacity is at the end of its useful life. The operator does not see the state of health directly, only diagnostics measured in the cycle, and a manufacturer that introduces a new chemistry has tested only a few cells of it. Part 2 gave the six cells of one chemistry the same degradation curve. That was a sensible first model, and its test showed the limit: predicted from the other five, four cells were followed closely and two were missed. Cells differ, and cells of one chemistry resemble each other more than they resemble cells of another, so the question is how far a new cell should be believed to resemble the cells that have been seen.
This post answers it with a hierarchical model, in which each cell draws its parameters from its chemistry and each chemistry from the whole fleet. The model is built with PyMC1 and fitted to the CALCE cycling data of Part 2, now with both chemistries. The post shows the priors before and after the data, checks how far the conclusions depend on the prior of the precision, and scores the model against its two obvious alternatives, one curve for all cells and one curve per cell, on the cells that it was fitted to. The hierarchy separates the two chemistries sharply. The second post of Part 3 tests it on two cells that it never saw and turns its predictions into the retirement decision of the operator.

title: Briefing a Data Science Team on the Problem and Not the Method
text:
The first post argued that a method prescribed from above costs a data science team three things: the knowledge that sits close to the data, its commitment to the result and the early report of a failure. The remedy is not to leave the team without direction. A brief that is written as a problem still states a great deal, and the leader keeps the choices that only the leader can make.
This post turns the argument into a division of the work. It sets out which of the three questions of a project belongs to leadership and which to the team, states the conditions under which the method should be specified after all, and describes three changes that a leader can make in practice. Like the first post, it rests on experience and on books on leadership, and its limits are stated in the last section.
